title: PGA Tour Tightens Fan Conduct Rules for 2027 Over Betting Worries
dek: The PGA Tour is revamping its fan code of conduct and deploying new security measures for the 2027 season in response to player concerns about sports betting-influenced fan behavior. The Tour will deploy trained ambassador volunteers in galleries and monitor online commentary for betting-related harassment.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Multiple PGA Tour players raised concerns during the 2026 season about sports betting's impact on fan conduct during competition, prompting the Tour to introduce an ambassador program and online monitoring ahead of 2027.
bottom_line: The Tour's new ambassador and online-monitoring programs take effect in 2027. How they function across all events, what specific behaviors will trigger ejection, and whether online tracking will lead to enforcement actions remain unresolved.
body: The PGA Tour is introducing a revamped fan code of conduct and new security measures for the 2027 season in response to player concerns about sports betting-influenced fan interference during competition. The shift reflects a deepening tension between preserving golf's gallery tradition and managing behavior that players fear could be tied to wagering.

Multiple PGA Tour players raised concerns during the 2026 season about the impact sports betting is having on professional golf, according to Front Office Sports. PGA Tour senior VP of tournament administration Andy Levinson said: "We are concerned about fans interacting with our players in a negative manner, and certainly the potential for fans to try to impact the competition in some way."

The Tour will deploy an ambassador program consisting of trained volunteers positioned in crowds to identify and report fans causing problems. It is also creating new programs to track and monitor online commentary from fans about players they have bet on, according to Front Office Sports. The Tour will add security measures to better control poor crowd behavior during the 2027 season.

Jordan Spieth raised the stakes in June, expressing concern about how susceptible golf is to fans impacting on-course action. "It may not last very long, but you could impact a shot if you wanted to," Spieth stated, according to Front Office Sports. Spieth suggested that US Open champion Wyndham Clark facing a hostile crowd at Shinnecock Hills could have been gambling-related. At the WM Phoenix Open in February, a content creator paid a fan 100 dollars to yell during the backswing of a golfer, per Front Office Sports.

Less than 5% of ejections at PGA Tour events in 2026 were from sports betting-related incidents, according to PGA Tour VP of gaming Scott Warfield, announced but not independently verified. Warfield said: "One is one too many for us and it's why we spent the summer talking to players getting their feedback on this, leading to some of the stuff we're looking at for 2027 with the tracking of harassing comments that usually start on the course, go online, or vice versa."

Levinson acknowledged the enforcement limits the Tour faces. "At the same time, if you've got 10,000 people standing around a green and somebody decides to blurt something out, those things are really hard to control," he said, per Front Office Sports. "So, we do rely on decorum a little bit at golf tournaments. In some markets we've seen that deteriorate."

The Tour has not yet partnered with a prediction market, and players are not allowed to sign sponsorship deals with prediction markets, announced but not independently verified. Warfield stated: "We'll get in when we're ready and when it's right for our members. It wasn't in 2026; we'll see what it is in 2027." The PGA Tour has concerns about prediction markets' regulatory status as the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and states jockey for control. There are ongoing lawsuits related to whether event contracts on prediction markets are legal financial trades or illegal sports bets. The USTA signed Kalshi as the exclusive prediction market of the US Open. The NFL and NBA have not yet made the prediction market leap, but the MLB and NHL have partnered with prediction markets, per Front Office Sports.
